summary: Discusses common reasons protocol implementations run slowly and how to organize them into modules without hurting efficiency. It is advice for implementers rather than a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary:
This memo asks a question that sounds odd today: does the tidy way of dividing a protocol into layers make it slower? David Clark's answer is yes, and the memo spends most of its length on where to put the cut so that you get tidiness and speed at the same time.

It is advice for people writing protocol code, not a specification of anything on the wire.

questions: should tcp run in the kernel
how to speed up tcp checksum
subtitle: Clark's 1982 case that neat layering costs speed, and how to structure a protocol implementation to get both.

tldr.problem: Protocol implementations often run far slower than their authors expected, and the blame is usually put on the protocol design or the operating system rather than on how the code was put together.
tldr.mechanism: The memo argues that the way a protocol is carved into modules and fitted into the operating system is the dominant factor, and that a firm boundary between layers costs performance that a carefully chosen cut does not.
tldr.outcome: It is advice for implementers rather than a protocol, and it is still Informational. It gives arithmetic for packet timing and cost figures from a real TCP implementation.

sections.title: Why Implementations Run Slow
sections.content:
Many protocol implementers have made the unpleasant discovery that their packages do not run quite as fast as they had hoped. The blame for this widely observed problem has been attributed to a variety of causes, ranging from details in the design of the protocol to the underlying structure of the host operating system.

Experience suggests that one of the most important factors in determining the performance of an implementation is the manner in which that implementation is modularized and integrated into the host operating system. The memo argues that modularity is one of the chief villains in attempting to obtain good performance, so that the designer is faced with a delicate and inevitable tradeoff between good structure and good performance. The single factor which most strongly determines how well this conflict can be resolved is not the protocol but the operating system.
sections.plainLanguage: The complaint is always that the protocol is too complicated, or that the operating system is in the way. Clark says look first at how the code is arranged and where it sits.

sections.title: What Efficiency Means
sections.content:
There are many aspects to efficiency. One is sending data at minimum transmission cost, which is a critical aspect of common carrier communications if not of local area network communications. Another is sending data at a high rate, which may not be possible at all if the net is very slow, but which may be the one central design constraint when taking advantage of a local net with high raw bandwidth. The final consideration is doing the above with minimum expenditure of computer resources. This last may be necessary to achieve high speed, but in the case of the slow net it may matter only in that the resources used up, for example CPU cycles, are costly or otherwise needed. These different goals often conflict; for example it is often possible to trade off efficient use of the computer against efficient use of the network. There may therefore be no such thing as a successful general purpose protocol implementation.

The simplest measure of performance is throughput, measured in bits per second. Assume that data is being sent from one machine to another in packets of 576 bytes, the maximum generally acceptable internet packet size. Allowing for header overhead, this packet size permits 4288 bits in each packet. If a useful throughput of 10,000 bits per second is desired, then a data bearing packet must leave the sending host about every 430 milliseconds. That is clearly not difficult to achieve. To achieve 100 kilobits per second the packet must leave the host every 43 milliseconds, and to achieve one megabit per second, which is not at all unreasonable on a high-speed local net, the packets must be spaced no more than 4.3 milliseconds apart.

Many operating systems take a substantial fraction of a millisecond just to service an interrupt. If the protocol has been structured as a process, it is necessary to go through a process scheduling before the protocol code can even begin to run. If any piece of a protocol package or its data must be fetched from disk, real time delays of between 30 and 100 milliseconds can be expected. If the protocol must compete for CPU resources with other processes, it may be necessary to wait a scheduling quantum before the protocol can run, and many systems have a scheduling quantum of 100 milliseconds or more. It becomes immediately clear that the protocol must be fitted into the operating system in a thorough and effective manner if any like reasonable throughput is to be achieved.

Except in very special circumstances, when many packets are being processed at once, the cost of processing a packet is dominated by factors such as CPU scheduling which are independent of the packet size. This suggests two general rules. First, send data in large packets, because if processing time per packet is a constant then throughput is directly proportional to the packet size. Second, never send an unneeded packet, since unneeded packets use up just as many resources as a packet full of data but perform no useful function.
sections.plainLanguage: Do the numbers first. To fill a megabit per second with 576-byte packets you must send one every 4.3 milliseconds, and a single disk read can cost thirty times that. The shape of the code matters more than how clever the protocol is.

sections.title: The Protocol and the Operating System
sections.content:
There are normally three reasonable ways in which to add a protocol to an operating system. The protocol can be in a process provided by the operating system, it can be part of the kernel of the operating system itself, or it can be put in a separate communications processor or front end machine. The decision is strongly influenced by details of hardware architecture and operating system design, and each approach has its own advantages and disadvantages.

In a process. This is the simplest path, and it has real advantages: since modifications to the kernel are not required, the job can be done by someone who is not an expert in kernel structure, which matters because it is often impossible to find somebody experienced in both the operating system and the protocol. The disadvantages relate to both structure and performance. Process scheduling can be a significant source of real-time delay, and the operating system may not have the right priority tools to bring the process into execution quickly whenever there is work to be done. Structurally, the difficulty is that the protocol may be providing services, such as support of data streams, which are normally obtained by going to special kernel entry points. The most extreme example is server telnet: in almost all systems the device handler for the locally attached teletypes is inside the kernel, so if server telnet is implemented in a process it becomes necessary to get the data streams back down inside the kernel so that they mimic the local teletype interface, which usually requires special kernel modification and so defeats the benefit of having removed the protocol from the kernel.

In the kernel. Structurally it is reasonable to view the network as a device, and device drivers are traditionally in the kernel, so scheduling problems can be sidestepped to some extent. But network protocols have a characteristic shared by almost no other device: they require rather complex actions to be performed as a result of a timeout, and the kernel often has no facility by which a program can be brought into execution as a result of a timer event. Failing that, the only execution mechanism available is to run at interrupt time. There are substantial drawbacks to this. The actions performed may be complex and time consuming compared with the maximum time the operating system is prepared to spend servicing an interrupt, and problems arise if interrupts are masked for too long, which is particularly bad when running as a result of a clock interrupt. The environment provided by an interrupt handler is usually extremely primitive compared with the environment of a process, and many system facilities are unavailable there. The most important of these is the ability to suspend execution pending the arrival of some event or message, and it is a cardinal rule of almost every known operating system that one must not invoke the scheduler while running in an interrupt handler. The system scheduler also has no control over the percentage of system time used by the protocol handler, so if a large number of packets arrive from a host that is either malfunctioning or fast, all of the time may be spent in the interrupt handler, effectively killing the system.

Two more problems with the kernel: the kernel address space may simply be too small to hold the code, so that for every byte of new feature put in, some other byte of old feature must be thrown out, and it is hopeless to expect an effective and general implementation under that constraint. And a protocol package thoroughly entwined in the operating system may need to be redone every time the operating system changes.

On a separate processor. The operating system on the communications processor can be tailored for precisely this kind of task, which makes the job much easier, and the task need not be redone for every machine the protocol is added to, so more attention can be paid to doing it right. The problems are financial, and more fundamental: because the communications processor is a separate machine it must be attached to the host by some mechanism, and whatever that mechanism, code is required in the host to deal with it. That interface package is still a protocol in nature, with all of the same structural problems, so all of the issues raised above must still be faced.
sections.plainLanguage: Three places to put the code: an ordinary program, inside the operating system, or on a second machine. Each one moves the same problems around rather than removing them.

sections.title: How to Slice the Layers
sections.content:
The decision of where to implement a protocol is more complicated than it looks, because the goal is not to implement a single protocol but a whole family of protocol layers: a device driver or local network driver at the bottom, then IP and TCP, and eventually the application specific protocol such as Telnet, FTP and SMTP on the top. The bottommost of these layers is somewhere within the kernel, since the physical device driver for the network is almost inevitably located there. The top layers, which give the user the ability to log in remotely or send mail, are not entirely contained within the kernel. The question is therefore not whether the protocol family shall be inside or outside the kernel, but how it shall be sliced in two between the part inside and the part outside.

Since protocols come nicely layered, an obvious proposal is that one of the layer interfaces should be the point at which the inside and outside components are sliced apart, and most systems have been implemented this way. One obvious place to slice is at the upper interface of TCP. Since TCP provides a bidirectional byte stream, which is somewhat similar to the I/O facility provided by most operating systems, it is possible to make the interface to TCP almost mimic the interface to other existing devices. Except in the matter of opening a connection and dealing with peculiar failures, the software using TCP need not know that it is a network connection rather than a local I/O stream. This puts TCP inside the kernel, however, which raises all the problems addressed above, and it also raises the problem that the interface to the IP layer can become excessively buried inside the kernel. Things other than TCP are expected to run on top of IP, so the IP interface must be made accessible even if TCP sits on top of it inside the kernel.

Another obvious place to slice is above Telnet, which solves the problem of having remote login channels emulate local teletype channels. The disadvantage is that the amount of code included in the kernel is getting remarkably large; in some early implementations the size of the network package, including protocols at the level of Telnet, rivals the size of the rest of the supervisor.

Any attempt to slice through a lower layer boundary, for example between Internet and TCP, reveals a fundamental problem. The TCP layer, as well as the IP layer, performs a demultiplexing function on incoming datagrams. Until the TCP header has been examined it is not possible to know for which user the packet is ultimately destined. If TCP as a whole is moved outside the kernel, it is necessary to create one separate process, the TCP process, which performs the TCP multiplexing function and probably all of the rest of TCP processing. Incoming data destined for a user process then involves not just a scheduling of the user process but scheduling the TCP process first.

This suggests an alternative structuring strategy which slices through the protocols not along an established layer boundary but along a functional boundary having to do with demultiplexing. Certain parts of IP and certain parts of TCP are placed in the kernel, enough that when an incoming datagram arrives it is possible to know for which process the datagram is ultimately destined. The datagram is then routed directly to the final process, where additional IP and TCP processing is performed. This removes from the kernel any requirement for timer based actions, since they can be done by the process provided by the user, and it reduces the amount of code required in the kernel, so that it is suitable for systems where kernel space is at a premium.
sections.plainLanguage: The question is not where to draw the line between layers, but where to draw it in the code. Clark suggests cutting the code at the point where the system has worked out which program a packet is for, and letting that program do the rest of the work.

sections.title: Breaking Down the Barriers
sections.content:
The result of the strategy above was that part of TCP should execute in the process of the user. Instead of one TCP process for the system, there is one TCP process per connection. Given this architecture it is no longer necessary to imagine that all the TCPs are identical. One TCP could be optimized for high throughput applications such as file transfer, and another for small low delay applications such as Telnet. It would even be possible to produce a TCP somewhat integrated with the Telnet or FTP on top of it. Such an integration is extremely important, because independent layers have independent ideas about when packets should be sent, and unless these layers can be brought into cooperation, additional packets will flow.

The best example is the operation of server telnet in a character at a time remote echo mode on top of TCP. When a packet containing a character arrives at a server host, each layer has a different response. TCP has an obligation to acknowledge the packet. Either server telnet or the application layer above has an obligation to echo the character received. If the character is a Telnet control sequence, then Telnet has additional actions it must perform. The result, in most implementations, is that several packets are sent back in response to the one arriving packet. Combining all of these return messages into one packet is important for several reasons. It reduces the number of packets being sent over the net, which directly reduces the charges incurred for many common carrier tariff structures. And it reduces the number of scheduling actions which will occur inside both hosts.

The way to achieve this goal of packet sharing is to break down the barrier between the layers of the protocols, in a very restrained and careful manner, so that a limited amount of information can leak across the barrier to enable one layer to optimize its behaviour with respect to the desires of the layers above and below it. For example, it would represent an improvement if TCP, when it received a packet, could ask the layer above whether it would be worth pausing for a few milliseconds before sending an acknowledgement, to see if the upper layer would have outgoing data to send. Dallying before sending the acknowledgement produces precisely the right sort of optimization if the client of TCP is server Telnet. It is, however, absolutely unacceptable if TCP is being used for file transfer, because in file transfer there is almost never data flowing in the reverse direction and the delay in sending the acknowledgement probably translates directly into a delay in obtaining the next packets. So TCP must know a little about the layers above it to adjust its performance as needed.

The general conclusion is that a layer boundary has both a benefit and a penalty. A visible layer boundary with a well specified interface provides a form of isolation between two layers which allows one to be changed with the confidence that the other will not stop working. However, a firm layer boundary almost inevitably leads to inefficient operation. The memo compares this with file systems, where a highly formalized interface makes it easy for naive users to get at disks without writing much software, but where the restricted interface almost inevitably leads to inefficiency, and where implementors of a database system almost inevitably attempt to reject the file system and obtain direct access to the disks, sacrificing modularity for efficiency.
sections.plainLanguage: Strict boundaries make each layer safe to change, and they also make every layer send its own packet. Letting a little information cross the boundary, and giving each connection its own tailored transport code, avoids that.

sections.title: Efficiency of Protocol Processing
sections.content:
IP is a simple protocol, especially with respect to the processing of normal packets, so it should be easy to get it to perform efficiently. The only area of complexity related to actual packet processing has to do with fragmentation and reassembly.

Most costs in the IP layer come from table lookup functions rather than packet processing functions. An outgoing packet requires two translation functions to be performed: the internet address must be translated to a target gateway, and a gateway address must be translated to a local network number. It is easy to build a simple implementation of these table lookups that in fact performs very poorly. The programmer should keep in mind that there may be as many as a thousand network numbers in a typical configuration, and linearly searching a thousand entry table on every packet is extremely unsuitable. It may even be worth asking TCP to cache a hint for each connection, which can be handed down to IP each time a packet is sent, to try to avoid the overhead of a table lookup.

TCP is a more complex protocol and presents many more opportunities for getting things wrong. One area is generally accepted as causing noticeable and substantial overhead: the computation of the checksum. It would be nice if this cost could be avoided, but the idea of an end-to-end checksum is absolutely central to the functioning of TCP, and no host implementor should think of omitting the validation of a checksum on incoming data. Various clever tricks have been used to minimize the cost of computing it. If it is possible to add additional microcoded instructions to the machine, a checksum instruction is the most obvious candidate. Since computing the checksum involves picking up every byte of the segment and examining it, it is possible to combine that operation with the operation of copying the segment from one location to another. Careful attention to the details of the algorithm used can make a drastic difference in throughput: the Multics system, a 36-bit word machine with four 9-bit bytes per word, laid the eight-bit bytes of a TCP segment down packed in memory ignoring word boundaries, so horrible masking and shifting was required for each 16-bit value. An early version of a program using this strategy required 6 milliseconds to checksum a 576-byte segment, and a more careful recoding of the algorithm reduced the checksum processing time to less than one millisecond.

Another area of TCP processing which may cause performance problems is the overhead of examining all of the possible flags and options in each incoming packet. The strategy the implementor ought to use is to build the program to optimize the expected case. A TCP should be built on the assumption that the next packet to arrive will have absolutely nothing special about it and will be the next one expected in the sequence space. One or two tests are sufficient to determine that the expected set of control flags are on: the ACK flag should be on, the Push flag may or may not be on, and no other flags should be on. One test is sufficient to determine that the sequence number of the incoming packet is one greater than the last sequence number received. Other data structures can be organized to optimize the action which is normally taken on them: the retransmission queue is very seldom actually used for retransmission, so it should not be organized to optimize that action but rather to optimize discarding things from it when the acknowledgement arrives, and in many cases the easiest way is not to save the packet at all but to reconstruct it only if it needs to be retransmitted.

A generality at least as important as optimizing the common case is to avoid copying data any more times than necessary. Multics takes between two and three milliseconds within the TCP layer to process an incoming packet, depending on its size. For a 576-byte packet the three milliseconds are used up approximately as follows: one millisecond computing the checksum, six hundred microseconds copying the data, which is copied twice at three hundred microseconds a copy, and seven hundred milliseconds on header processing and packet resequencing, with the rest in miscellaneous processing. Data copying is the second most expensive single operation after data checksuming. Some implementations, often because of an excessively layered modularity, end up copying the data around a great deal, and others copy the data because there is no shared memory between processes, so the data must be moved from process to process via a kernel operation.
sections.plainLanguage: The last few tenths of a millisecond are won by small choices: check the expected case first, look things up in a hash rather than a list, and copy the bytes as few times as you can.

viz.caption: The three places a protocol can live, and what each costs

cells: No kernel changes needed, so anyone can write it
Scheduling problems can be sidestepped, and the network can be treated as a device
The operating system can be tailored to the task, and the work need not be redone per host
Process scheduling delay, and services that normally come from kernel entry points
Timeouts are awkward, the kernel address space is small, and the code may need redoing when the OS changes
The host still needs code to talk to the processor, and that interface is itself a protocol

items.title: Optimize the expected case
items.text: Assume the next packet is an ordinary one with the next sequence number, and check for that first.

items.title: Do not copy the data more than necessary
items.text: Copying is the second most expensive operation after the checksum, and too much layering causes a lot of it.

items.title: Do not use a linear table search
items.text: A routing table may hold a thousand network numbers, and searching it on every packet is unsuitable.

items.title: Organize each structure for what usually happens
items.text: The retransmission queue is rarely used for retransmission, so organize it for discarding acknowledged packets.
